speeds up a reaction without being used up

bullets: Test drops with iodine every minute
When iodine stays orange, starch has gone

lessons.unit: Spring 1: Combustion (8E); light (8J)
lessons.title: Burning fuels
lessons.bigQuestion: Where does a candle go when it burns?
objectives: To understand combustion as a reaction between a fuel and oxygen that releases energy
successCriteria: All: name the reactants and products of burning a hydrocarbon
Most: write a word equation for complete combustion
Some: explain why mass seems to be lost when a fuel burns
lessons.crossCurricular: Geography: fossil fuels and energy supply
lessons.smsc: Spiritual: fuels as Allah's provision stored in the earth

keywords.def: burning: a fuel reacting with oxygen
a substance that releases energy when burned
a compound of hydrogen and carbon only
a substance that reacts
a substance made in a reaction

hook.text: A candle gets shorter as it burns. Where has the wax gone?
hook.a: It reacts with oxygen and becomes carbon dioxide and water vapour, which escape into the air.

islamicLink.text: Allah says: 'Have you seen the fire that you kindle? Is it you who produced its tree, or are We the Producer?' (al-Waqi'ah 56:71-72). Fire and fuels are gifts from Allah that we must use carefully.

starter.q: Name the gas in air we need to burn things.
Write the chemical formula of water.

teach.heading: Fuel + oxygen
bullets: Hydrocarbons make carbon dioxide and water

model.problem: Write a word equation for burning methane
steps: Reactants: methane + oxygen
Products of a hydrocarbon: carbon dioxide + water
methane + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water

teach.heading: Testing the products
bullets: Water: blue cobalt chloride paper turns pink (or anhydrous copper sulfate turns blue)
teach.note: Teacher demo video: candle under a funnel, gases drawn through a cooled tube and limewater.

teach.heading: Where does the mass go?
bullets: If we collected them, the mass would increase
teach.note: Answer the big question: oxygen from the air is added, so the products weigh more than the wax that burnt.

misconception.wrong: Burning destroys matter
misconception.right: Atoms are rearranged into gases; mass is conserved

check.q: A gas turns limewater milky. It is…
check.why: Limewater is the test for carbon dioxide. Water is tested with cobalt chloride or copper sulfate.

practice.q: Write the word equation for propane burning completely.
practice.model:
Reactants: the fuel (propane) and oxygen.
Products of any hydrocarbon burning completely: carbon dioxide and water.
So propane + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water.

practice.q: How do we test for water?
practice.a: Blue cobalt chloride paper turns pink (or white anhydrous copper sulfate turns blue).

practice.q: Is combustion exothermic or endothermic?

independent.q: Core: Write word equations for burning methane, butane and hydrogen.
independent.a: methane + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water; butane + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water; hydrogen + oxygen → water.
independent.model:
Teacher writes methane first: methane + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water.
Hydrocarbon in, carbon dioxide and water out.

independent.q: Extend: Why does hydrogen make no carbon dioxide when it burns?
independent.a: It contains no carbon atoms.

independent.q: Stretch: A candle on a balance loses mass as it burns. Explain why this does not break the law of conservation of mass. Write in the portal response box.
independent.a: The products (carbon dioxide and water vapour) escape as gases; if collected, the total mass of products would equal the wax and oxygen used.

exit.q: The products of complete combustion of a hydrocarbon are...
Big question: where does a candle go when it burns?
exit.a: The wax reacts with oxygen to form carbon dioxide and water vapour, which escape into the air.

lessons.homework: List four fuels used in or near your home and write a word equation for one.
lessons.send: SEND: word equation frame with cards. EAL: fuel, burn, product. Stretch: balance the symbol equation for methane: CH₄ + 2O₂ → CO₂ + 2H₂O.

Most: write word equations for metals reacting with oxygen
Some: use conservation of mass to calculate the mass of oxygen gained

keywords.def: a reaction where a substance gains oxygen
a compound of an element with oxygen
mass is not created or destroyed in a reaction
slow oxidation of iron with water and oxygen
gives out energy

hook.text: Magnesium ribbon burns with a blinding white light and the ash weighs more than the ribbon. Where did the extra mass come from?
hook.a: From oxygen in the air, which joined the magnesium.

starter.q: Products of complete combustion of methane?

starter.a: A compound of hydrogen and carbon only.

teach.heading: Oxidation
teach.note: Show magnesium ribbon burning (video; bright light, do not look directly).

teach.heading: Mass increases
bullets: Magnesium oxide weighs more than magnesium

model.problem: 2.4 g of magnesium burns to make 4.0 g of magnesium oxide. What mass of oxygen reacted?
steps: Mass is conserved
Oxygen = product − magnesium

teach.heading: Burning vs rusting
bullets: Rusting is slow and needs water too

misconception.wrong: Magnesium loses mass when it burns, like wood
misconception.right: It gains oxygen, so the solid product is heavier

check.q: What forms when copper is heated in air?
check.why: Copper + oxygen → copper oxide. Heating in air supplies oxygen.

practice.q: 3.6 g magnesium makes 6.0 g magnesium oxide. Mass of oxygen?
practice.model:
Mass is conserved.
Oxygen = product - metal.
6.0 - 3.6 = 2.4.
So 2.4 g of oxygen reacted.

practice.q: Write the word equation for iron reacting with oxygen.
What two things does iron need to rust?

independent.q: Core: Write word equations for copper, zinc and calcium reacting with oxygen.
independent.a: copper + oxygen → copper oxide; zinc + oxygen → zinc oxide; calcium + oxygen → calcium oxide.
independent.model:
Teacher writes copper first: copper + oxygen → copper oxide.
Metal + oxygen → metal oxide.

independent.q: Extend: 6.4 g copper gains 1.6 g oxygen. What mass of copper oxide forms?
Stretch: Explain why wood ash weighs less than the wood but magnesium oxide weighs more than magnesium.
independent.a: Wood's products are mostly gases that escape; magnesium oxide is a solid that keeps the oxygen it gained.

exit.q: Oxidation means...
Big question: why does magnesium get heavier but wood lighter when burned?
exit.a: Magnesium gains oxygen into a solid oxide; wood's products are gases that escape.

lessons.homework: Find one example of rusting at home or outside and explain how it could have been prevented.
lessons.send: SEND: metal + oxygen → metal oxide pattern card. EAL: oxide, gain, rust. Stretch: write balanced symbol equations: 2Mg + O₂ → 2MgO.

keywords.def: a solution that turns milky with carbon dioxide

what we see, hear or measure

hook.text: A glass held above a candle mists up. A jar placed over a candle puts it out. What two clues do these give?
hook.a: The mist shows water is a product; the flame going out shows oxygen is used up.

starter.a: Cobalt chloride paper turns blue to pink

teach.heading: Teacher demonstration
bullets: Then a jar over the candle
teach.note: Teacher only, on camera. Pupils do not light candles for this lesson.

teach.heading: Observations
bullets: Flame goes out under the jar

teach.heading: Common error

misconception.right: It uses some of the oxygen (about 21% of air); most of the air is nitrogen, which does not burn

check.q: The cold glass above the candle mists up. This shows...
check.why: Water vapour from combustion condenses on the cold glass.

practice.q: Doubling the jar volume roughly... the burning time.
practice.a: Doubles (8 s to 17 s to 35 s).
practice.model:

500 to 1000, time 17 to 35, about double.
So time is roughly proportional to volume: more oxygen, longer burn.

practice.q: Is 'the glass misted' an observation or an inference?

practice.a: Too little oxygen is left to keep it burning.

independent.q: Core: Write up the demonstration: equipment, observations, inferences and the word equation for paraffin wax burning.
independent.a: Observations and inferences as above; wax + oxygen → carbon dioxide + water.
independent.model:
Teacher writes the first line: 'Observation: a cold glass held above the flame misted up.

hook.text: A smooth lake shows a perfect upside-down picture of the trees, but a choppy lake does not. Why?

starter.a: Light reflects off it into our eyes.

bullets: Angle of incidence = angle of reflection
teach.note: Draw the normal as a dashed line at 90°.

steps: Angles are measured from the normal
Law: i = r

teach.heading: Common error
bullets: Measure from the normal, not the mirror

misconception.wrong: The ray hits at 40° to the mirror, so i = 40°
misconception.right: Measure from the normal: i = 90° - 40° = 50°

teach.heading: Specular and diffuse

check.q: Angle of incidence is 50°. Angle of reflection?
check.why: The law of reflection: i = r.

practice.q: A ray hits a mirror at 20° to the surface. Find the angle of reflection.
practice.model:
The 20° is from the mirror, not the normal. i = 90 - 20 = 70°.
Law: r = i.
So r = 70° from the normal.

practice.q: Why can't you see a reflection in a wall?
practice.a: Its rough surface gives diffuse reflection, scattering light.

practice.q: What is the normal?
practice.a: A line at 90° to the surface where the ray hits.

independent.q: Core: Draw three ray diagrams with angles of incidence 30°, 45° and 60° and measure the reflected angles.
independent.a: Reflected angles 30°, 45°, 60° from the normal.
independent.model: Teacher draws the first: mirror line, dashed normal, incident ray at 30°, reflected ray at 30° on the other side.

independent.q: Extend: Explain why road signs use rough, matt paint but mirrors are polished.
independent.a: Matt paint gives diffuse reflection so signs are seen from many angles without glare; mirrors need specular reflection for a clear image.

independent.q: Stretch: Two mirrors at 90°. A ray hits the first at 30° to the normal. Find the angle it leaves the second mirror.
independent.a: It reflects at 30°, meets the second mirror at 60° to its normal, leaves at 60°, travelling back parallel to its original path.

exit.q: Angles in reflection are measured from the...
Big question: why can you see yourself in a mirror but not in a wall?
exit.a: The mirror is smooth (specular reflection, a clear image); the wall is rough (diffuse reflection scatters light).

lessons.title: Home practical: measuring reflection with a mirror

how close a measurement is to the true value
a difference between measured and true values
a narrow gap making a thin beam

hook.text: If you measured i = 40° and r = 43°, does that mean the law is wrong?
hook.a: Probably not: small errors in drawing and measuring explain a few degrees.

starter.a: Light scattered by a rough surface.

teach.heading: Equipment
bullets: Torch with card slit (or a phone torch)
teach.note: Make a slit: tape card over the torch with a 2 mm gap.

teach.heading: Method
bullets: Draw the mirror line and a normal
Shine the ray along a drawn incident line
Mark the reflected ray with two dots
cycle: Draw incident ray at a set angle

teach.heading: Safety
bullets: Never shine the torch into eyes

check.q: Which change would most improve accuracy?
options: A thinner beam and sharp pencil
check.why: A thin beam and fine lines make the ray positions precise.

practice.q: Using the table, do the results support the law? Explain.
practice.a: Yes: each difference is 2° or less, within measuring error.
practice.model:
Compare each pair: 20/21, 40/39, 60/62, 70/70.
Differences are 0 to 2 degrees.
These are small and random, so they are measurement errors.
So the results support i = r.

practice.q: Name one source of error.
practice.a: Wide beam, thick pencil lines, reading the protractor.

practice.q: Why repeat each angle?
practice.a: To spot anomalies and take a mean.

independent.q: Core: Carry out the practical at four angles (20°, 40°, 60°, 70°) and record i and r.
independent.a: Pupils' own; r within a few degrees of i.
independent.model: Teacher shows the first measurement on camera: incident line at 20°, shine, dot, join, measure r = 21°.

independent.q: Extend: Write a conclusion and evaluation in the portal response box. Start: 'My results show...'
independent.a: My results show r was within 2° of i each time, supporting the law; errors came from the beam width.

independent.q: Stretch: Suggest how a phone camera could give a more accurate record.
independent.a: Photograph from directly above the paper, then measure angles on screen.

exit.q: i = 55°, r measured as 56°. Best conclusion?
Big question: does the law of reflection really work?
exit.a: Yes: measured r matched i within small measurement errors.

options: speeds up, bends away from normal

practice.q: Light leaves glass into air at an angle. Which way does it bend?
practice.a: Away from the normal (it speeds up).
practice.model:
New medium: air, less dense than glass.
Light speeds up.
Speeding up bends it away from the normal.

practice.q: Why does a ray along the normal not bend?

practice.q: How many times faster is light in air than in glass (chart)?

independent.q: Extend: Explain why a swimming pool looks shallower than it really is (portal response box).
independent.a: Light from the bottom bends away from the normal at the surface; we trace rays back in straight lines, so the bottom appears higher.

independent.q: Stretch: Explain refraction with the 'marching soldiers' model.
independent.a: When one side of a row reaches slower ground first it slows, so the row turns towards the normal.

exit.q: Light slows down entering glass and bends...

exit.a: Light from the straw refracts as it leaves the water, so the underwater part appears in a different place.
